title: A prime has exactly two divisors, so the Bool primality predicate answers true
statement: If n is prime -- 2 <= n and every divisor of n is 1 or n -- then the Bool predicate Nat.isPrime, which decides primality by counting the divisors of n among 1..n and comparing that count to 2, answers true at n.

formal.statement: theorem Nat.isPrime_eq_true_of_prime : ((x0 : AxNat) -> ((x1 : And (AxNat.le (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) x0) (((x1 : AxNat) -> ((x2 : AxNat.dvd x1 x0) -> Or (Eq.{1} AxNat x1 (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) (Eq.{1} AxNat x1 x0))))) -> Eq.{1} Bool (AxNat.isPrime x0) Bool.true))

evidence.supports: prime_condition n implies Nat.isPrime n = true
evidence.checker_command: test "$(cargo run -q -p axeyum-lean-kernel --example nat_theorem_inventory -- 'Nat.isPrime_eq_true_of_prime' 2>/dev/null | grep -xFc 'Nat.isPrime_eq_true_of_prime	4	((x0 : AxNat) -> ((x1 : And (AxNat.le (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) x0) (((x1 : AxNat) -> ((x2 : AxNat.dvd x1 x0) -> Or (Eq.{1} AxNat x1 (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) (Eq.{1} AxNat x1 x0))))) -> Eq.{1} Bool (AxNat.isPrime x0) Bool.true))')" -ge 1
evidence.notes: `Nat.isPrime n` unfolds to `beq (countRange (fun j => beq (n % (j+1)) 0) n) 2` -- a divisor COUNT, not a trial division. The proof shows that count is exactly two for a prime: `1 | n` supplies the index 0, `Nat.mod_self` supplies the index n-1, and every index between is refuted by primality's own divisor clause (`c = 1` by `succ_ne_zero`, `c = n` by `lt_irrefl` against the range hypothesis). The count is assembled by peeling the last index with `countRange_succ_of_true` and the first with `countRange_split` at 1, leaving `countRange_eq_zero_of_all_false` for the middle: 2 = 1 + 0 + 1. The rendered type is matched in full because the weakening that matters here is invisible to a name check: `Nat.isPrime` is universe- and argument-compatible with any `AxNat -> Bool`, so a checker that read only the name would be satisfied by a theorem about a different predicate entirely.

evidence.supports: axiom_footprint: [] -- the Nat prelude's trusted surface is empty
evidence.notes: `nat_axiom_inventory` bounds the footprint by enumerating the whole trusted surface: a theorem cannot depend on a trusted declaration the environment does not contain. All three kinds are covered -- counting `Declaration::Axiom` alone would not suffice, because `Opaque` has no proof body and `Quotient` admits `Quot.sound`. The module's own test `the_prime_counting_shelf_is_admitted_and_axiom_free` additionally asserts `Environment::contains` BEFORE reading the footprint, because `axiom_footprint` returns an empty set for a name that was never declared.

provenance.source: statement authored here against this kernel's own vocabulary; nothing copied

notes: The keystone of the prime-counting shelf. `prime_counting.rs` declared `Nat.isPrime` under ADR-0653 as a CONSTRUCTION ONLY, with no theorem about it, and a shape_search over the whole environment (declarations=3277) for anything whose type mentions `Nat.isPrime` returned ABSENT. So before this nothing connected the Bool predicate that `Nat.primeCounting'` actually counts to this prelude's propositional `prime_condition`, and every source of primes in the kernel (`Nat.exists_prime_gt`, `Nat.exists_prime_dvd`, `Nat.min_fac_prime`) produces the latter. Monotonicity was landable without it only because monotonicity is true of `countRange` at an arbitrary predicate. ONLY THE FORWARD DIRECTION IS PROVED. The converse -- `isPrime n = true` implies `prime_condition n` -- is a different argument (a count of two forces the divisor set to be exactly {1, n}, which needs a pigeonhole on the count rather than two witnesses) and is NOT claimed here.
